rows.subtype: Stage 1: The juicy piece of news [Actor]
rows.description: A child sees a classmate crying near the office and hears a fragment about her family. Feeling important for knowing something others do not, she is eager to tell it.
She tells her best friend, adding a detail to make it more interesting. Children often mix what they saw with what they guessed, and the guess sounds truer each time it is told.
The story travels in whispers with "do not tell anyone". A listener joins in to feel part of the group, and repeating it becomes a way of belonging.
The girl notices stares and giggles, learns what is being said and feels shame and anger. She wants to hide or hit back, and her confusion is greater because the story is partly false.

rows.subtype: Stage 5: A bystander stops the chain [Response]
rows.description: A classmate says "I do not want to talk about this, it is her business" and does not pass it on. Rumours need carriers, and even one child refusing to repeat them shortens the life of the story.
The teacher talks with the class about how words hurt, without naming the girl, and offers her a trusted adult to talk to. The child learns that saying the truth calmly is stronger than whispering.
A toddler is told it is time to leave the park. He cannot manage the wish to stay, so his face crumples, his body stiffens and he starts to cry.
He drops to the floor, screams, kicks and may throw things or arch his back. He cannot listen or reason, since the brain areas for calming are still very immature.

rows.subtype: Stage 3: Caregiver's stress and choice point [Observer]
rows.description: The caregiver feels embarrassment, anger or tiredness with strangers watching. The choice is to shout, to give in, or to stay calm and safe nearby, and staying calm is the hardest and the most useful.
The caregiver kneels, says in a low voice "You are upset. I am here", moves harmful objects aside and waits. Presence without argument tells the toddler that big feelings are survivable.
The crying becomes sobs, and he reaches out with arms open or leans in. He now needs comfort, not a lecture, and a hug, a drink of water and a slow breath help his body settle.

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Repair and naming the feeling [Response]
rows.description: Later, in simple words: "You wanted to stay. That was hard. We can come again tomorrow." The limit stays, the love is clear, and the toddler slowly learns words for feelings.

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Public teasing meets a raw spot [Receiver]
rows.description: In the group chat a teenager is teased about his marks, and it lands on a fear that he is not good enough. He replies quickly, before thinking, because silence would feel like admitting it.

Classmates start reacting with emojis and screenshots, and the argument becomes a show. Both teens now defend their reputation with an audience watching, which makes backing down feel like a public loss.
Friends join in on each side and repeat things said in private. What was a two-person quarrel becomes two camps, and the original hurt is buried under loyalty and taking sides.
After a day of sulking the teen realises he is more hurt about being laughed at than about anything said. The anger drains, and he wonders how to step back without looking weak.
A private, brief message such as "That got out of hand. Can we talk tomorrow, just us?" moves the argument out of the audience. Speaking face to face, away from the group, removes most of the fuel.

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
rows.description: Each says what they regret without demanding the other apologise first. A mature repair keeps friendship above who started it, and the group cools when the two of them do.
